root_cause: refundTicket (lines 549-561) is a permissionless function that requires only a valid ticketId. It looks up the user from _ticketOwner(ticketId) (line 554) and sends ticketSize to that user. Unlike refund() and refundSelf(), it does not require the commitment preimage (outcomeId, amount, payout, salt). This is by design for cancelled markets - it allows anyone to trigger refunds for any ticket. The security relies on: (1) the phase being Cancelled, (2) claimedTickets[ticketId] preventing double-refund, (3) funds going to the recorded commitmentUsers[ticketId] (not to the caller). However, this means that if commitmentUsers[ticketId] is an address that cannot receive ERC20 tokens (e.g., a contract that reverts on receive), the refund would fail and the user's funds would be stuck until the refund deadline passes and are swept. This is a minor liveness concern, not a security vulnerability.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is cancelled
Step 2: Anyone calls refundTicket(ticketId) for any valid ticketId
Step 3: Funds are sent to commitmentUsers[ticketId] (the recorded ticket owner)
Step 4: If that address is a contract that reverts on ERC20 transfer, the refund is stuck
preconditions: Market is Cancelled
User address is a contract that reverts on token receipt

title: RelayerEscrow._commitAuthorizationHash: Assembly hash uses abi.encode-equivalent 32-byte-padded words, mismatch with off-chain encodePacked computation causes DoS
root_cause: Lines 270-282 use raw assembly to hash 9 words (9*32 = 288 bytes = 0x120). Addresses (self, market, user) are stored via mstore which left-pads them to 32 bytes with zeros. This is equivalent to abi.encode behavior, not abi.encodePacked. The view helper commitAuthorizationHash (line 177-183) calls the same internal function, so off-chain clients can precompute the hash. However, if an off-chain client independently recomputes the hash using abi.encodePacked(address,address,bytes32,uint256,address,uint256,uint256,uint256,uint256) instead of using the view helper, the resulting hash will be different because encodePacked uses 20 bytes for addresses instead of 32. This is not a vulnerability in the contract itself but in integration correctness.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: An off-chain SDK computes the authorization hash using abi.encodePacked instead of abi.encode for addresses
Step 2: The hash mismatch causes approveCommitAuthorization to store a hash that differs from what commitOnBehalf computes
Step 3: The commit is rejected with CommitAuthorizationMissing
preconditions: Off-chain client uses wrong encoding (abi.encodePacked instead of abi.encode-style for addresses)

title: RevealMarket.lockBatches: Settlement timeout (14 days) is measured from lockedAt, but if lockBatches is called right at commitDeadline, the full 14 days must pass before cancellation, during which pool funds are locked
root_cause: lockBatches (line 376) sets lockedAt = block.timestamp. enableRefunds from Locked phase (line 484) requires block.timestamp >= lockedAt + SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (14 days). During these 14 days, pool.reservedLiability[market] and reservedTotal hold the reserved amount, reducing pool idle liquidity. This is the designed settlement window. The concern is whether 14 days is appropriate for the pool's liquidity needs. With many concurrent markets, each locking liquidity for up to 14 days, the pool could be heavily reserved. This is an economic design parameter, not a code bug. The pool's capacity mechanism (capacityEnabled/capacityLimit) provides the owner with a knob to control total exposure. If capacity is set, reserveLiability checks capacity (line 127), preventing over-commitment.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Pool has 100000 balance. 10 markets each reserve 10000. reservedTotal = 100000. Idle = 0
Step 2: All 10 markets locked within a short window. Settlement timeout is 14 days each
Step 3: LPs cannot withdraw anything for up to 14 days (until at least one market settles or cancels)
Step 4: New markets cannot get pool reservations (no idle liquidity)
preconditions: Many markets locked concurrently
Pool capacity fully reserved

title: MarketFactory.setRelayerCommitsPaused: Asymmetric error handling between pause and unpause can leave relayers in inconsistent pause states
root_cause: _setRelayerCommitsPausedBatch (line 554-582) has asymmetric error handling: when pausing (line 563-566), it calls setCommitsPaused(true) and then VERIFIES commitsPaused() returns true, reverting on failure. When unpausing (line 567-579), failures are swallowed with try/catch and events emitted. This means if a relayer's setCommitsPaused(false) call reverts (e.g., the relayer escrow has been bricked or upgraded), the unpause continues for other relayers but that specific relayer remains paused. The factory has no mechanism to remove a bricked relayer from the activeRelayers array, so subsequent pause/unpause operations will continue to encounter this relayer. The only workaround is for the owner to deactivate the relayer by rotating all its markets away, which decrements the refcount to 0 and removes it from activeRelayers.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Three relayers R1, R2, R3 are active with markets assigned
Step 2: Owner calls setRelayerCommitsPaused(true) -- all three pause successfully
Step 3: R2 becomes a bricked contract (via selfdestruct by a proxy admin, or its owner calls a destructive function)
Step 4: Owner calls setRelayerCommitsPaused(false) to unpause all relayers
Step 5: R1 and R3 unpause successfully; R2's unpause call reverts (swallowed), R2 remains paused forever
Step 6: Markets assigned to R2 cannot accept commits because R2.commitsPaused() returns true (checked in RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization line 283)
preconditions: A relayer escrow becomes non-functional (bricked proxy, storage corruption, etc.)
That relayer is still in the activeRelayers array

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketProtocolPool: registerMarket on new pool creates fresh liabilityCap entry but old pool retains stale entry with non-zero reservedLiability if rotation happens after partial lifecycle
root_cause: updateMarketProtocolPool (line 339-351) has the guard `rm.phase() != IRevealMarket.Phase.Commit || rm.nextTicketId() != 0` at line 346 (revert ProtocolPoolRotationLocked). This ensures the market is in Commit phase with zero tickets. Since reserveLiability is called during lockBatches (which transitions from Commit to Locked), and the market has 0 tickets (so no lock is possible), reservedLiability on the old pool should be 0 for this market. The new pool's registerMarket (ProtocolPool line 98-105) sets reservedLiability[market] = 0, consumedLiability[market] = 0, and liabilityCap[market] = cap. However, the old pool is not cleaned up: its allowedMarket[market] = true, liabilityCap[market] = old cap, but consumed/reserved should both be 0 (since no commits were made). The dangling allowedMarket on the old pool means the market address could theoretically still call old_pool.reserveLiability() or old_pool.draw(), but the market's protocolPool storage now points to the new pool, so it would never make those calls.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market M registered on poolA with cap 100
Step 2: Owner rotates M to poolB while in Commit phase with 0 tickets
Step 3: poolA has allowedMarket[M]=true, liabilityCap[M]=100, consumed=0, reserved=0
Step 4: M.protocolPool = poolB; M will only interact with poolB going forward
Step 5: poolA's stale entries are cosmetic but could affect capacity accounting if poolA enables capacity tracking
preconditions: Market must be in Commit phase with 0 tickets (enforced by ProtocolPoolRotationLocked)

title: ProtocolPool._burnUnlockedShares: FIFO burn skips locked deposits but total deducted from lpShareBalance which includes locked shares
root_cause: In lpWithdraw (line 249-270), the check at line 251 is `sharesToRedeem > lpShareBalance[msg.sender]` — this checks against the TOTAL share balance including locked shares. But _burnUnlockedShares (line 381-396) only burns from unlocked deposits. If sharesToRedeem exceeds unlocked shares but is less than total lpShareBalance, the lpShareBalance check at line 251 passes, but _burnUnlockedShares reverts at line 395 with InsufficientUnlockedShares. This is safe (the revert catches it) but the check ordering means the more specific error (InsufficientUnlockedShares) is thrown from deep in the call stack rather than at the entry point. No actual vulnerability — just a UX concern where the initial check is looser than necessary.
trigger_scenario: LP has 100 shares total: 60 unlocked, 40 still locked.
LP calls lpWithdraw(80, 0). lpShareBalance check: 80 <= 100, passes.
convertToAssets(80) = 80 (assuming healthy pool). Slippage passes.
_burnUnlockedShares tries to burn 80 from unlocked deposits, only finds 60. remaining = 20.
Reverts with InsufficientUnlockedShares. No fund loss, but check ordering could be tighter.
preconditions: LP has both locked and unlocked deposits
LP tries to redeem more than unlocked portion

title: RevealMarket.verifyAndSettleBatched: no finalization if not all batches verified in single call allows indefinite partial settlement blocking refunds
root_cause: verifyAndSettleBatched (line 442) only calls _finalizeSettlement when settledBatchCount == batchCount. If the oracle submits proofs for all-but-one batch, the market remains in Phase.Locked indefinitely. The enableRefunds function (line 484) allows cancellation after lockedAt + SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (14 days). So users are protected by the timeout mechanism. However, an adversarial oracle could repeatedly call verifyAndSettleBatched with incomplete batch sets, and each call accumulates accumulators without resetting them (since epoch doesn't change). The accumulators for already-verified batches persist because batchProofEpoch prevents re-verification of the same batch. So this is actually the designed incremental settlement. The oracle can submit N-1 batches in one call, then 1 batch in the next call, and finalization occurs. This is correct behavior. The 14-day timeout ensures the oracle cannot stall indefinitely.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market locked with 5 batches.
Step 2: Oracle calls verifyAndSettleBatched with batches [0, 1, 2, 3]. settledBatchCount = 4.
Step 3: Oracle never submits batch 4.
Step 4: After lockedAt + 14 days, anyone can call enableRefunds via the factory.
Step 5: Market transitions to Cancelled and users can refund.
preconditions: Oracle is adversarial or experiences operational failure.
Multi-batch market.

title: RevealMarket.verifyAndSettle: publicSignals[4] (totalLiability) not checked against on-chain state enables ZK-circuit-dependent liability
root_cause: In verifyAndSettle, the public signals are validated: signals[0] == batchRoots[0], signals[1] == marketId, signals[2] == winningOutcomeId, signals[3] == totalEscrow, signals[5] == rakeBps, signals[8] == circuitHash, signals[9] == 0. Notably, signals[4] (totalLiability), signals[6] (poolTotalYes), and signals[7] (poolTotalNo) are NOT validated against on-chain state -- they are circuit outputs. The ZK circuit is the sole authority for these values. If the circuit is sound, this is correct by design: the circuit computes payouts from the commitment data. However, this makes the protocol entirely dependent on circuit soundness for the most critical financial computation. The contract-level defense is the invariant check in _finalizeSettlement: poolYes_ + poolNo_ == totalLiability_ (line 741) and totalLiability_ <= totalEscrow_ + protocolLiabilityCap (line 748). These constrain the damage surface but don't independently verify correctness.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Sound circuit: totalEscrow = 100, totalLiability = 80 (losing side escrow subsidizes winners).
Step 2: Buggy circuit: totalEscrow = 100, totalLiability = 150 (inflated beyond actual payouts).
Step 3: Contract draws 50 from pool (deficit = 150 - 105 balance after rake).
Step 4: Contract holds 155. surplus = 155 - 150 = 5 sent to pool.
Step 5: 150 available for claims. If actual winning payouts are only 80, 70 would go unclaimed and be swept to pool.
Step 6: Protocol pool bears a larger draw than necessary.
preconditions: ZK circuit must have a soundness bug that inflates totalLiability.
Oracle must submit the malicious proof.

title: RevealMarket.sweepUnclaimed: Race between claim and sweep if factory unpauses then sweeps in same block
root_cause: sweepUnclaimed (line 817) checks: phase == Settled, deadline passed, not already swept, recipient == protocolPool. It then sets claimsPaused = true and claimsSwept = true (lines 823-824), and transfers the entire remaining balance. A race could occur if: (1) claims are paused, (2) the effective deadline passes while paused (impossible because _effectiveClaimDeadline extends during pause), (3) factory unpauses claims and in the same transaction sweeps. Actually, examining _effectiveClaimDeadline more carefully: when unpaused, claimPauseTotalDuration is updated with the elapsed pause time (line 726), so the effective deadline extends. For sweep to succeed, block.timestamp must exceed the new effective deadline (claimDeadline + claimPauseTotalDuration). After unpausing, claimPauseTotalDuration has been incremented to account for the pause, so the effective deadline jumped forward. If the factory unpauses and the new effective deadline is already in the past, then both sweep and claim could theoretically execute in the same block. But sweep sets claimsSwept = true before the transfer (line 824), and claim checks claimsSwept (line 460). Since both are externally called (not in the same tx), the ordering depends on transaction ordering. If sweep executes first, claim would revert. If claim executes first, sweep would transfer less. This is the expected design - first come first served within the deadline window.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market settles, claims are paused for 200 days
Step 2: Factory unpauses claims - claimPauseTotalDuration = 200 days, effective deadline = claimDeadline + 200 days
Step 3: If current time already exceeds claimDeadline + 200 days, both sweep and late claims are possible
Step 4: In a race, transaction ordering determines whether users can still claim
preconditions: Market Settled
Claims were paused long enough that unpause + totalDuration is already past deadline

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: Nonce replay prevention does not enforce ordering, allowing backend to selectively deny commits by pre-burning nonces
root_cause: Line 293 checks usedCommitNonces[auth.user][auth.nonce] which prevents replay of the same nonce for the same user on the same market. Nonces are unbounded uint256 values with no ordering enforcement. The backend signer can issue signatures with any nonce value. If a malicious or compromised backend pre-submits a commit for a user's nonce (burning it), the user's intended commit with that nonce will fail with CommitReplay. However, the backend already controls commit ordering and is trusted by design (NatSpec line 270-272). The nonce space is 2^256, so exhaustion is infeasible. Additionally, the user must have approved the authorization hash (which includes the nonce) on the escrow, so the backend cannot burn a nonce without a matching user approval.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Backend issues a signed CommitAuth with nonce=5 for user Alice on market M
Step 2: The commit succeeds and usedCommitNonces[Alice][5] = true
Step 3: Backend accidentally re-signs with nonce=5 for Alice on the same market
Step 4: Second commit reverts with CommitReplay
preconditions: Backend nonce management has a bug that produces duplicate nonces for the same user-market pair

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketVerifier: Verifier rotation during Commit phase with existing commitments allows circuitHash to remain unchanged, but new verifier may compute different proof outputs for same commitments
root_cause: RevealMarket.setVerifier (line 674-683) at line 679 checks: `if (commitments.length != 0 && newCircuitHash != circuitHash) revert CircuitHashMismatch()`. This prevents changing the circuitHash if there are existing commitments. However, it ALLOWS changing the verifier address to a different verifier contract with the SAME circuitHash but potentially different verifying key material (different IC points, different alpha/beta/gamma/delta). Two different verifier contracts can have the same circuitHash but different verifying keys, meaning proofs valid under one verifier would be invalid under the other. The factory's _validateVerifier checks approvedVerifier[newVerifier] and codehash/keyHash match, ensuring the new verifier is approved. But if the new verifier has a different verifying key (different keyHash), then proofs generated for the old verifier would fail. This is operationally risky but not a security vulnerability since the owner must approve both verifiers and the off-chain prover must generate proofs for the correct verifier.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market M has verifier V1 with circuitHash C and keyHash K1; 50 commitments exist
Step 2: Owner deploys verifier V2 with circuitHash C but keyHash K2 (different trusted setup)
Step 3: Owner approves V2 and calls updateMarketVerifier(M, V2, C)
Step 4: setVerifier allows this because circuitHash is unchanged (same C)
Step 5: At lock time, lockedVerifierKeyHash is set to K2
Step 6: Off-chain prover must now use V2's trusted setup to generate proofs; old proofs for K1 are invalid
preconditions: Two approved verifiers share the same circuitHash but have different verifying keys
Market has existing commitments

title: ProtocolPool.setCapacity: Capacity reset while markets have consumed (not reserved) liability creates phantom capacity
root_cause: setCapacity (line 200-206) requires `reservedTotal == 0` before allowing capacity changes. However, it does not account for consumedLiability across markets. If markets have drawn funds (consumedLiability > 0) but released their reservations (reservedTotal == 0), the owner can set a new capacity that does not reflect past draws. Capacity tracks a global risk budget, but consumed draws have already reduced actual pool balance. If capacity is set to pool balance but consumedLiability has already transferred funds out, the capacity budget could authorize more draws than the pool can service. However, each draw individually checks `amount > balance - reservedTotal` (unreserved path, line 167), so the actual balance check prevents overdraw regardless of capacity value.
trigger_scenario: Pool has 100 ZEN. Markets have consumed 40 ZEN (pool balance now 60). reservedTotal = 0.
Owner calls setCapacity(100). capacity = 100, capacityLimit = 100.
New market tries draw(60). capacity check: 60 <= 100, passes. Balance check: 60 <= 60, passes.
Pool balance is 0 but capacity still shows 40 remaining. Next draw would fail on balance check.
No actual over-draw occurs due to balance check, but capacity is misleading.
preconditions: Markets have consumed liability (drawn funds)
Owner resets capacity after draws complete

title: RevealMarket._verifyBatchProof: per-batch totalEscrow signal not validated against on-chain per-batch expected escrow, enabling proof forgery to manipulate liability split
root_cause: In _verifyBatchProof (lines 857-872), the per-batch signals[3] (escrow), signals[4] (liability), signals[6] (poolYes), signals[7] (poolNo) are NOT individually validated against any on-chain per-batch expected values. They are accumulated into settledEscrowSum, settledLiabilitySum, etc. The only aggregate check is at line 443: settledEscrowSum != totalEscrow. This means the per-batch escrow/liability distribution is trusted entirely to the ZK circuit. The ZK proof for each batch attests that signals[3..7] are correct for the given Merkle root (signals[0]) and the other fixed parameters. Since the Merkle root is checked against batchRoots[batchIndex] (line 857), and the proof is verified, the per-batch values must be consistent with the commitments in that batch. However, if the ZK circuit has a soundness bug (e.g., allows the prover to arbitrarily assign escrow/liability across batches as long as totals match), an attacker with access to the oracle key could manipulate the per-batch split. This is a trust-in-circuit issue, not a contract bug. The contract's aggregate totalEscrow check provides a final consistency gate.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market with 2 batches. On-chain totalEscrow = 100.
Step 2: Valid circuit behavior: batch 0 escrow = 60, batch 1 escrow = 40.
Step 3: Hypothetical circuit bug: prover claims batch 0 escrow = 0, batch 1 escrow = 100, with different liability splits.
Step 4: Both proofs pass Groth16 verification if the circuit is buggy.
Step 5: settledEscrowSum = 100 == totalEscrow, check passes. But liability split is wrong.
Step 6: _finalizeSettlement receives wrong settledLiabilitySum affecting pool draw amount.
preconditions: ZK circuit has a soundness vulnerability allowing arbitrary per-batch signal values.
Oracle colludes or is compromised.

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Oracle signature binding to winningOutcomeId prevents cross-market replay but allows pre-signing before settlement
root_cause: The oracle signature digest includes address(this), marketId, ticketId, user, winningOutcomeId, payout, expiry, block.chainid (lines 585-596). The inclusion of address(this) and block.chainid prevents cross-market and cross-chain replay. The inclusion of winningOutcomeId means the oracle must sign after the result is known. However, there are only 2 possible outcomes (0 or 1), so an oracle could pre-sign authorizations for both outcomes. The attacker (or a compromised oracle) would only use the one matching winningOutcomeId after settlement. The expiry field limits the temporal window. The on-chain check on line 574 (phase != Settled) ensures the claim can only execute after settlement. This is not a vulnerability per se, but it means oracle authorization signatures can be prepared in advance if both outcome variants are signed.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Before settlement, oracle signs CLAIM_ORACLE_V1 for ticketId=0 with winningOutcomeId=0, payout=X, expiry=far_future
Step 2: Oracle also signs CLAIM_ORACLE_V1 for ticketId=0 with winningOutcomeId=1, payout=Y, expiry=far_future
Step 3: Market settles with winningOutcomeId=1
Step 4: The signature for outcome=1 is now valid and can be used
Step 5: The signature for outcome=0 would fail because winningOutcomeId check in digest would produce wrong signer
preconditions: Oracle signs both outcome variants in advance

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: Refund after cancellation returns full ticketSize including rake, creating insolvency if rake was separately extracted
root_cause: In commitWithAuthorization (line 316-319), the contract splits ticketSize into rake and net: totalEscrow += net, rakeCollected += rake. The market contract's token balance equals ticketSize * numCommitments. In the cancellation path (refundTicket, refund, refundSelf), each refund pays back the full ticketSize (lines 520, 543, 558). Since no tokens are extracted between commit and cancellation (enableRefunds does not transfer rake), the market holds exactly ticketSize * N tokens. Refunding all N tickets at ticketSize each results in 0 remaining. However, if any mechanism extracted rake before cancellation (e.g., a future code path or admin function), refunds would be underfunded. Currently no such extraction path exists in the Cancelled phase flow, so this is safe by invariant. The key invariant is: no tokens leave the market between commit and cancellation.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: 100 users commit with ticketSize=100 and rakeBps=500 (5% rake)
Step 2: Market holds 10,000 tokens. totalEscrow=9,500, rakeCollected=500
Step 3: Market is cancelled via enableRefunds()
Step 4: All 100 users claim refunds of 100 each = 10,000. Market balance reaches 0. Solvent.
Step 5: (Hypothetical) If rake was extracted before cancellation, only 9,500 tokens available for 10,000 in refunds. Last 5 users can't refund.
preconditions: A code path that extracts rake before cancellation is introduced in a future upgrade
Currently no such path exists so the invariant holds

title: RelayerEscrow.recoverExcessCollateral: Race condition with creditMigrated allows double-accounting of excess tokens
root_cause: Both recoverExcessCollateral (lines 221-226) and creditMigrated (lines 206-213) rely on _excessCollateral() to determine available unassigned tokens. _excessCollateral returns COLLATERAL_TOKEN.balanceOf(this) - accountedCollateral. If the factory calls creditMigrated in the same block as the owner calls recoverExcessCollateral, both could see the same excess and try to use it. However, creditMigrated increases accountedCollateral while recoverExcessCollateral transfers tokens out (reducing the balance). If creditMigrated is called first, the excess decreases, and recoverExcessCollateral may revert with InsufficientCollateralBacking. If recoverExcessCollateral is called first, the token balance decreases, and creditMigrated may revert. Either way, only one can succeed for the same tokens. The nonReentrant guard on recoverExcessCollateral prevents reentrancy but doesn't protect against sequential calls in the same block by different callers (owner vs factory).
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Someone sends 1000 tokens directly to the escrow (creating excess collateral)
Step 2: Owner submits recoverExcessCollateral(recipient, 1000) in the same block as factory submits creditMigrated(user, 1000)
Step 3: Only the first transaction to be included succeeds; the second reverts with InsufficientCollateralBacking
Step 4: No double-spend occurs, but operational coordination is needed
preconditions: Owner and factory both attempt to use excess collateral in the same block

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketRelayer: Old relayer unregistration failure is silently caught, leaving allowedMarket[market]=true on old relayer, enabling stale commitOnBehalf calls to the old relayer for this market
root_cause: In updateMarketRelayer (lines 288-290), the factory tries to unregister the market from the old relayer via `RelayerEscrow(payable(oldRelayer)).unregisterMarket(market)`. If this reverts, it catches the error and emits RelayerUnregisterFailed, but continues. The market's relayerEscrow is then updated to the new relayer (line 293). After rotation, the old relayer still has allowedMarket[market]=true. However, commitOnBehalf on the old relayer cannot succeed because: (1) the old relayer calls IRevealMarket(market).commitWithAuthorization which has `onlyRelayer` modifier checking msg.sender == relayerEscrow, and relayerEscrow now points to the new relayer. So the old relayer's commitOnBehalf would transfer tokens to the market but the market.commitWithAuthorization call would revert with NotRelayer. BUT: the _safeTransferExact in commitOnBehalf (line 153) happens BEFORE the external call to market.commitWithAuthorization (line 154). If the market call reverts, the entire transaction reverts (no try/catch). So the token transfer is also rolled back. The old relayer's commitOnBehalf would revert entirely. The stale allowedMarket entry is a cosmetic issue, not a fund risk. Still, creditFromMarket on the old relayer could be called by the market (since allowedMarket is still true), but the market would only call creditFromMarket if it were paying users through escrow, which is not the current design.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market M is on Relayer A. allowedMarket[M]=true on Relayer A
Step 2: Factory owner rotates to Relayer B. unregisterMarket on A fails (silently caught). allowedMarket[M] still true on A
Step 3: Market's relayerEscrow now points to B

Step 4: Relayer A's owner tries commitOnBehalf(user, M, ...). Transfers ticketSize to M. Calls M.commitWithAuthorization. M checks msg.sender == relayerEscrow (B). Reverts NotRelayer. Entire tx reverts. Funds safe
Step 5: However, if market M somehow calls A.creditFromMarket(user, amount), it would succeed since allowedMarket[M]=true on A. This requires M to approve and transfer tokens to A first
preconditions: Relayer rotation with unregistration failure on old relayer
Old relayer must still be operational

title: MarketFactory.setVerifierApproval: Verifier owner can rotate key material after approval, breaking pinning invariant until next isVerifierCurrentlyApproved call
root_cause: setVerifierApproval (line 179-206) pins codehash and keyHash at approval time and stores them in approvedVerifierCodehash/approvedVerifierKeyHash. The Verifier contract allows the owner to call setVerifyingKey at any time (Verifier.sol line 77-86), which changes verifyingKeyHash and circuitHash in the Verifier contract's storage. This does NOT change the Verifier's codehash (bytecode is immutable). However, it changes the keyHash returned by verifyingKeyHash(). The runtime check isVerifierCurrentlyApproved (line 220-232) compares verifier.verifyingKeyHash() against approvedVerifierKeyHash[verifier], so a key rotation will cause the verifier to fail the runtime check. This is the intended design (drift detection). However, the window between key rotation and the next settlement attempt is unguarded -- during this window, the verifier is still marked approvedVerifier[verifier] = true in storage, but will fail runtime checks. This is actually correct behavior, not a vulnerability.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Owner approves verifier V with keyHash K1
Step 2: Owner (same entity) rotates V's verifying key to K2 via Verifier.setVerifyingKey()
Step 3: approvedVerifier[V] is still true, but isVerifierCurrentlyApproved returns false because keyHash K2 != approvedVerifierKeyHash K1
Step 4: All markets using V are unable to lock or settle until owner re-approves (requires clearVerifierPin first since codehash unchanged but keyHash changed)
preconditions: Verifier owner (same as factory owner due to ownership check) rotates verifying key after approval

title: MarketFactory.createMarket: Deterministic clone salt uses only marketId, enabling address prediction and potential contract interaction before official registration
root_cause: cloneDeterministic at line 459 uses `bytes32(marketId)` as the salt. Since nextMarketId is a public sequential counter (starting at 1, line 38), the next market's address can be predicted by anyone calling predictMarketAddress(nextMarketId). While the clone cannot be front-run (only the factory can deploy via cloneDeterministic), tokens could be sent to the predicted address before the market exists. Since the clone is an ERC-1167 proxy, any tokens sent to the address before deployment would be accessible by the market after deployment (the market can interact with its own token balance). However, RevealMarket's commitWithAuthorization checks `IERC20(collateralToken).balanceOf(address(this)) < totalEscrow + ticketSize` (line 287), so pre-sent tokens could satisfy this balance check without the escrow actually transferring tokens. This could let a relayer commit without transferring the ticket amount if pre-funded tokens are present.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Attacker reads nextMarketId = 42 and calls predictMarketAddress(42) to get predicted address P
Step 2: Attacker sends 1000 collateral tokens to address P
Step 3: Factory creates market 42 at address P via createMarket
Step 4: Market now has 1000 pre-funded tokens in its balance
Step 5: RelayerEscrow.commitOnBehalf transfers ticketSize to market, but market's balance check passes even if transfer somehow fails or is short (unlikely with safeTransfer)
Step 6: Pre-funded tokens would be swept as surplus during _finalizeSettlement or remain in the contract
preconditions: Attacker pre-funds the predicted market address with collateral tokens
Tokens must be the correct collateral token

title: RevealMarket.verifyAndSettleBatched: partial batch settlement across multiple transactions allows stale accumulator state if epoch is not advanced between calls
root_cause: verifyAndSettleBatched (line 422) can be called multiple times to incrementally verify batches. The per-batch replay protection uses batchProofEpoch[batchIndex] == currentBatchProofEpoch (line 856). Between two calls to verifyAndSettleBatched, the oracle could call refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash which increments currentBatchProofEpoch and resets all accumulators (lines 695-700). This is correct behavior. However, consider the scenario where between two verifyAndSettleBatched calls (without an epoch reset), the verifier key is rotated by the Verifier owner. The market checks IVerifier(verifier).verifyingKeyHash() != lockedVerifierKeyHash (line 431/854), which would cause the second call to revert. The factory must call refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash first. This is working as designed -- the epoch mechanism correctly invalidates partial progress. No bug found in this flow.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Oracle calls verifyAndSettleBatched with batches 0-2 of 5 total batches. Accumulators are partially filled.
Step 2: Verifier owner rotates the verifying key via setVerifyingKey.
Step 3: Oracle calls verifyAndSettleBatched again for batches 3-4. This reverts at line 431 because verifyingKeyHash changed.
Step 4: Factory must call refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash, which resets accumulators and increments epoch.
Step 5: Oracle must re-prove all batches 0-4 with the new key.
preconditions: Multi-batch market in partial settlement.
Verifier key rotation occurs mid-settlement.

title: RevealMarket.verifyAndSettle: single-batch path validates signals[3] == totalEscrow but batched path only checks aggregate -- circuit could assign wrong per-batch escrow in batched flow
root_cause: In verifyAndSettle (single-batch, line 409), signals[3] is checked against on-chain totalEscrow. In _verifyBatchProof (batched flow), signals[3] is NOT checked per-batch -- it is accumulated into settledEscrowSum (line 869), and only the final sum is checked against totalEscrow (line 443). This means each batch's reported escrow is trusted from the ZK proof. A valid ZK proof for a given batch root proves that the escrow amount is consistent with the commitments in that batch's Merkle tree. However, if different batches report overlapping or inflated escrow values that happen to sum to totalEscrow, the individual batch escrow values could be wrong while the total is correct. The ZK circuit should prevent this if it correctly computes escrow from the leaves. But the contract has no per-batch on-chain escrow value to cross-check. This is by design -- per-batch escrow depends on the commitments in each batch, which are only available inside the circuit. The aggregate check provides a final consistency gate.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: 2-batch market. Batch 0 has commits totaling 60 ZEN escrow, batch 1 has 40 ZEN.
Step 2: Circuit correctly reports: batch 0 escrow = 60, batch 1 escrow = 40. Sum = 100 == totalEscrow.
Step 3: Buggy circuit might report: batch 0 escrow = 30, batch 1 escrow = 70. Sum = 100 == totalEscrow.
Step 4: Per-batch liability would then also be wrong, but sum might be adjusted to compensate.
Step 5: Final totalLiability could be incorrect if per-batch liability errors don't cancel out.
preconditions: Circuit soundness bug allowing per-batch value manipulation.
Values must still sum to correct totalEscrow.

title: RevealMarket.lockBatches: batch count validation allows last batch to have fewer than BATCH_SIZE elements but Merkle tree depth is fixed at 8 -- padding leaves must be handled by prover
root_cause: lockBatches validates that the last batch's count may be less than BATCH_SIZE (lines 355-357). The Merkle tree has fixed depth 8, meaning 2^8 = 256 leaves. For the last batch with fewer commitments, the remaining leaves must be zero-padded in the Merkle tree. The prover is responsible for this padding. The _verifyLeaf function (line 910) checks `indexInBatch >= batchCounts[batchIndex]` to reject claims for padding slots. This means padding leaves cannot be claimed, even if someone knew the zero-padded leaf value. However, the ZK circuit must also handle padding correctly -- it must not include padding leaves in escrow/liability calculations. If the circuit treats zero-padded leaves as real commitments with zero amounts, this is fine (adds 0). If the circuit mishandles padding, per-batch values could be wrong. This is a circuit-level concern, not a contract bug. The contract-level guards (totalEscrow check, batchCounts check) provide defense-in-depth.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market with 300 commitments. Batch 0: 256 leaves, batch 1: 44 leaves + 212 padding.
Step 2: Merkle tree for batch 1 has 44 real leaves and 212 zero-padded leaves.
Step 3: ZK circuit computes escrow/liability for batch 1 over all 256 leaves including padding.
Step 4: Padding leaves should contribute 0 to escrow/liability.
Step 5: If circuit includes non-zero contributions from padding, per-batch values are wrong.
Step 6: Contract checks: settledEscrowSum == totalEscrow (post-hoc). Padding-induced errors would cause mismatch.
preconditions: Last batch has fewer than 256 commitments.
Circuit must correctly handle Merkle tree padding.

title: RevealMarket.claim: Missing validation that payout <= totalLiability per individual claim allows single claim to exceed totalLiability
root_cause: In the Merkle claim path (claim function, lines 448-474), there is no per-ticket check that payout <= totalLiability. The only check is the cumulative one: claimedLiability += payout followed by claimedLiability > totalLiability (lines 469-470). This means a single ticket could have a payout equal to or greater than totalLiability if the ZK proof and Merkle tree contain such a value. However, the ZK circuit is supposed to enforce that the sum of all payouts equals totalLiability (as checked in _finalizeSettlement: poolYes + poolNo == totalLiability). If the circuit correctly computes payouts, no single ticket's payout should exceed totalLiability. The contract trusts the ZK proof for this. In contrast, claimWithOracleAuthorization does check payout <= totalLiability per ticket (line 579). This asymmetry means the Merkle path relies entirely on the ZK proof correctness for per-ticket bounds, while the oracle path has an explicit on-chain guard. If the ZK circuit has a bug allowing inflated per-ticket payouts, the Merkle path would only catch it at the cumulative level.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: ZK circuit has a bug that allows one ticket's payout to exceed totalLiability
Step 2: The Merkle tree and proof are constructed with this inflated payout
Step 3: User calls claim() with the inflated payout value
Step 4: claimedLiability += inflated_payout exceeds totalLiability
Step 5: Reverts at line 470 (OverClaimed) - the cumulative guard catches it
preconditions: ZK circuit bug allowing per-ticket payout > totalLiability
Valid Merkle proof for the inflated leaf

title: RevealMarket.setClaimsPaused: Multiple pause/unpause cycles accumulate duration correctly but cap may be reached prematurely
root_cause: In setClaimsPaused (lines 719-736), when unpausing (paused=false, claimsPaused=true), the elapsed time (block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt) is added to claimPauseTotalDuration, which is capped at MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION (365 days). The concern is whether multiple short pauses that total more than 365 days could incorrectly cap individual pause segments. Examining the code: each unpause calculates elapsed = block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt (line 725), then newTotal = claimPauseTotalDuration + elapsed (line 726), capped at MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION (lines 727-729). This is correct: it tracks cumulative pause time across all pause/unpause cycles, and the total is capped at 365 days. A malicious factory could rapidly pause/unpause to reset the clock, but the cumulative tracking prevents gaming. The test testClaimPauseTotalDurationCapped confirms a single 400-day pause is capped at 365 days.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Factory pauses claims for 200 days, unpauses. claimPauseTotalDuration = 200 days
Step 2: Factory pauses claims for 200 more days, unpauses. elapsed=200, newTotal=400, capped to 365 days
Step 3: claimPauseTotalDuration = 365 days (MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION)
Step 4: Any further pauses still add to active duration in _effectiveClaimDeadline but not to the accumulated total
preconditions: Market is Settled
Multiple pause/unpause cycles

title: RevealMarket.refund: onlyRelayerOrFactoryOwner allows relayer owner to bypass factory admin controls for refunds
root_cause: The refund() function uses onlyRelayerOrFactoryOwner modifier (line 509). The _onlyRelayerOrFactoryOwner check (lines 223-229) allows msg.sender to be: (1) relayerEscrow contract, (2) relayerEscrow.owner(), or (3) factory.owner(). The relayer owner (relayerEscrow.owner()) is a separate key from the factory owner. If the relayer key is compromised, the attacker can call refund() directly for any ticket in a Cancelled market, which sends ticketSize to the recorded user. However, this only sends funds to the legitimate ticket owner, so a compromised relayer cannot steal funds - they can only trigger refunds to the rightful owners. The only harm would be forcing refunds earlier than intended, which is actually beneficial to users. The refundSelf and refundTicket paths don't require relayer authorization at all, so the relayer permission on refund() is additive, not restrictive.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is cancelled
Step 2: Compromised relayer owner calls refund(user, ticketId, ...) with correct preimage
Step 3: ticketSize is sent to the legitimate user (recorded in commitmentUsers)
Step 4: No theft possible since funds go to the registered ticket owner
preconditions: Market is Cancelled
Relayer owner key compromised
Attacker knows commitment preimage

title: RevealMarket.extendClaimDeadline: Window-open check uses _effectiveClaimDeadline but extension is relative to base claimDeadline creating asymmetric deadline semantics
root_cause: In extendClaimDeadline (line 795): the check uses _effectiveClaimDeadline() to determine if the window is still open, but the extension bounds check on line 797 uses the base claimDeadline: newDeadline > claimDeadline + MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION. And line 798 sets claimDeadline = newDeadline. This means: if claimPauseTotalDuration is large, the effective deadline could be far in the future even though the base claimDeadline is in the past. The factory could extend while the effective window is open but the base deadline has passed. After extension, the new effective deadline = newDeadline + claimPauseTotalDuration. The maximum new base deadline is old_claimDeadline + MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION (365 days), so the maximum effective deadline is old_claimDeadline + 365 + claimPauseTotalDuration (capped at 365 from unpause, but unlimited from active pause). In the worst case with an active pause, the effective deadline could be extremely far in the future. However, this all requires factory cooperation (they control pauses and extensions), so this is admin-controlled behavior.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: claimDeadline = T + 180 days, claims paused at T + 1 day
Step 2: At T + 200 days, base deadline (T+180) has passed but effective deadline = (T+180) + 0 + (T+200 - (T+1)) = T+180+199 = T+379
Step 3: Factory calls extendClaimDeadline(T + 180 + 365 = T + 545) - passes open check since T+200 < T+379
Step 4: New claimDeadline = T + 545, effective = T+545 + 0 + (T+200 - (T+1)) = T+744 (if still paused)
preconditions: Market Settled
Claims paused
Factory extends deadline

title: RelayerEscrow._commitAuthorizationHash vs RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: Different hash domain fields may allow authorization reuse across escrow migration
root_cause: The user-side authorization hash (_commitAuthorizationHash) binds to address(this) (escrow address) + market address + commitment fields, while the backend ECDSA signature binds to address(this) (market address) + marketId. If the factory calls setRelayerEscrow to rotate the escrow (line 658-662, no phase guard), a previously approved authorization hash for a user on the old escrow cannot be reused because the hash includes the old escrow address. However, the factory can deploy a new escrow with the same address via CREATE2, or if the authorization hash for the new escrow matches (i.e., same address), approvals could carry over. In practice, since _commitAuthorizationHash includes address(this) (the escrow), and the old escrow's storage is separate from the new escrow, old approvals are safely isolated. This is informational only.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Factory deploys EscrowV1 and user approves an authorization hash on EscrowV1
Step 2: Factory calls market.setRelayerEscrow(escrowV2) to rotate escrow
Step 3: The authorization hash on EscrowV1 is orphaned because EscrowV1 is no longer the market's relayer
Step 4: Even if EscrowV2 has same address (via CREATE2), the approval mapping is on a fresh contract with empty storage
preconditions: Factory performs an escrow rotation via setRelayerEscrow

title: RelayerEscrow.commitOnBehalf: External call to market after balance deduction allows state inconsistency if market reverts silently
root_cause: In commitOnBehalf (lines 149-154), the escrow first deducts balances[user] and accountedCollateral (lines 151-152), then transfers tokens to the market (line 153), then calls market.commitWithAuthorization (line 154). If commitWithAuthorization reverts, the entire transaction reverts, restoring the deducted balances. The nonReentrant guard prevents reentrancy. However, the function uses an external call to IRevealMarket(market).commitWithAuthorization. If the market contract is malicious (despite passing _isValidMarket checks during registration) and does not revert but silently fails (e.g., returns without storing the commitment), the escrow has already deducted the user's balance and transferred tokens. The user loses their ticket value but has no commitment stored. However, the market is registered by the factory via registerMarket, which calls _isValidMarket checking factory(), relayerEscrow(), and collateralToken(). A malicious market would need to be deployed by the factory, which requires factory owner control.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Factory owner deploys a market contract that passes _isValidMarket checks but has a modified commitWithAuthorization that doesn't store the commitment
Step 2: Relayer calls commitOnBehalf for a user on this market
Step 3: User's balance is deducted, tokens transferred, but no commitment is stored in the market
Step 4: User has no way to claim or refund because their ticket doesn't exist in the market
preconditions: Factory owner is malicious or compromised
Factory deploys a malicious market contract

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: Balance check uses totalEscrow (net of rake) not totalEscrow + rakeCollected, allowing a discrepancy window
root_cause: Line 287 checks: IERC20(collateralToken).balanceOf(address(this)) < totalEscrow + ticketSize. Here totalEscrow is the cumulative net amount (ticketSize - rake) across all previous commits. The actual token balance of the market is ticketSize * numPreviousCommits (full tickets). The check requires balance >= totalEscrow + ticketSize, which is weaker than requiring balance >= totalEscrow + rakeCollected + ticketSize (full accounting). This means the check would pass even if the actual balance was less than the full expected amount (totalEscrow + rakeCollected + ticketSize), as long as it exceeds totalEscrow + ticketSize. In practice, since the escrow always transfers the full ticketSize, the actual balance equals ticketSize * N, which always exceeds totalEscrow + ticketSize = net*(N-1) + ticketSize. The weaker check is sufficient but not tight. If tokens were somehow removed from the market between commits (which shouldn't happen in normal flow), this check could miss the discrepancy.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: 10 commits at ticketSize=100, rakeBps=1000 (10%). totalEscrow=900, rakeCollected=100, balance=1000
Step 2: Somehow 50 tokens are removed from the market (e.g., via a token with admin burn)
Step 3: Balance is now 950. Check: 950 >= 900 + 100 = 1000. This fails. The check catches it.
Step 4: Actually, if only 49 tokens removed, balance=951. Check: 951 >= 900 + 100. Fails. Still catches it.
Step 5: The check is actually totalEscrow + ticketSize, not totalEscrow + rakeCollected + ticketSize. 951 >= 900 + 100 = 1000. Still fails.
Step 6: For the 11th commit: check is 950 >= 900 + 100 = 1000. Fails correctly.
preconditions: Tokens are removed from the market contract between commits via external means (e.g., admin token burn, deflationary token)

title: RelayerEscrow.commitOnBehalf: User authorization hash does not include marketId, allowing potential confusion if market contract is redeployed at same address
root_cause: The _commitAuthorizationHash (lines 256-284) includes the market contract address but NOT the market's marketId. If a market contract is destroyed and a new one is deployed at the same address (via CREATE2) with a different marketId, a user's pre-existing approval from the old market could be valid for the new market at the same address, provided all other hash fields match (commitment, ticketId, user, nonce, expiry, ticketValue, chainId). However, the backend ECDSA signature in commitWithAuthorization (line 295-311) DOES include marketId, so even if the escrow authorization passes, the market-side signature verification would fail unless the backend issues a new signature for the new marketId. The dual-gate prevents exploitation but the missing marketId in the user authorization hash is a design gap.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: User approves authorization for market at address X with marketId=1
Step 2: Market at address X is destroyed and redeployed at same address with marketId=2
Step 3: User's approval on the escrow is still valid because the hash only includes the address, not marketId
Step 4: However, the backend ECDSA signature for the new market must include marketId=2, which won't match the old signature covering marketId=1
Step 5: commitWithAuthorization reverts with InvalidSignature on the new market
preconditions: Market contract is destroyed and redeployed at the same address via CREATE2
User has a pre-existing authorization approval

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: commitments array can grow up to MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT (16384) without gas limit concern on reads
root_cause: Line 288 caps commitments.length at maxCommitments (<= MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT = 16384). Each commit appends to both commitments[] and commitmentUsers[] arrays (lines 314-315). Reading these arrays (e.g., commitmentAt, _ticketOwner) uses direct index access which is O(1). The lockBatches function iterates over counts array (at most MAX_LOCK_BATCH_COUNT = 64 batches), not the commitments array. So gas consumption for read operations remains bounded. The primary gas concern is the lockBatches function which iterates and pushes up to 64 batch roots, but this is within acceptable gas limits.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market receives 16384 commits, filling commitments[] array
Step 2: lockBatches processes 64 batches of 256 commitments each
Step 3: Each commit is O(1) gas for push, each read is O(1) for index access
preconditions: Market reaches MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT

title: RevealMarket.refund: Refund pays ticketSize (gross) while totalEscrow tracked net of rake, leaving market insolvent for full refunds
root_cause: In commitWithAuthorization (line 316-318), totalEscrow accumulates `ticketSize - rake` (the net amount), and rakeCollected accumulates the rake. However, in refund/refundSelf/refundTicket (lines 520, 543, 558), the refundAmount is always `ticketSize` (the gross amount). When the market is cancelled after commits, the market contract holds `totalEscrow + rakeCollected` tokens in total. For N tickets: totalEscrow = N*(ticketSize - rake), rakeCollected = N*rake, so balance = N*ticketSize. Each refund pays ticketSize, so N refunds pay N*ticketSize. The accounting is actually balanced by the full token balance, not by totalEscrow. This is correct because the market holds the full ticketSize per ticket. However, if any tokens are donated or swept out before refunds complete, or if the surplus transfer mechanism in _finalizeSettlement has already moved tokens, the refunds could be underfunded. In the cancelled path specifically: enableRefunds calls _releaseLiabilityReservation but does NOT forward surplus to the pool. The market retains its full token balance. So under normal conditions this is sound. HOWEVER: if the market transitions from Locked to Cancelled (via enableRefunds after SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS), the pool.reserveLiability was already called during lockBatches. enableRefunds calls _releaseLiabilityReservation which releases the reservation. No pool draw occurred. No tokens moved. The market holds exactly N*ticketSize. Refunds pay N*ticketSize. This appears solvent. Belief lowered because the accounting appears correct for the cancel path.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market created with rakeBps=200 (2%), ticketSize=100
Step 2: 10 users commit via escrow. Market holds 1000 tokens. totalEscrow=980, rakeCollected=20
Step 3: Commit deadline passes, oracle locks batches. pool.reserveLiability called for protocolLiabilityCap
Step 4: SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (14 days) passes without settlement
Step 5: Factory owner calls enableMarketRefunds. Phase -> Cancelled. _releaseLiabilityReservation releases pool reservation
Step 6: All 10 users call refundTicket. Each gets ticketSize=100. Total payout = 1000 = market balance. Solvent.
Step 7: (Deviation) If an external actor somehow sends tokens to market or if partial settlement occurred before cancel, the accounting could diverge
preconditions: Market has been locked (phase=Locked) with non-zero rake
Settlement times out and refunds are enabled

title: RevealMarket._verifyBatchProof: settledEscrowSum accumulates per-batch escrow values from ZK proof signals without verifying they match per-batch commitment counts, enabling forged batch totals
root_cause: In _verifyBatchProof (lines 869-872), the function accumulates signals[3] (escrow), signals[4] (liability), signals[6] (poolYes), signals[7] (poolNo) from each batch proof into settledEscrowSum, settledLiabilitySum, settledPoolYesSum, settledPoolNoSum. After all batches are verified, verifyAndSettleBatched checks settledEscrowSum == totalEscrow (line 443). The ZK circuit is responsible for ensuring each batch's escrow equals the sum of (ticketSize - rake) for commitments in that batch. If the ZK circuit is sound, this sum across all batches will equal totalEscrow. However, the on-chain code does NOT independently verify that each batch's signals[3] corresponds to the expected escrow for that batch (batchCounts[i] * netTicketSize). It relies entirely on the ZK proof's soundness for this invariant. If the ZK circuit has a bug where batch-level escrow can be arbitrarily distributed across batches (e.g., one batch claims all escrow, others claim zero) but the sum is correct, the per-batch liability/poolYes/poolNo could also be skewed. But since only the sum matters for _finalizeSettlement and the sum check is performed (line 443), the aggregate invariant holds if the circuit is sound. The real question is whether the circuit enforces per-batch correctness.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market has 3 batches with 256, 256, and 100 commitments
Step 2: Oracle posts result. Oracle submits batched proofs
Step 3: Batch 0 proof has signals[3]=totalEscrow (all escrow attributed to batch 0), signals[4]=totalLiability
Step 4: Batch 1 and 2 proofs have signals[3]=0, signals[4]=0
Step 5: ZK verifier accepts all three proofs (depends on circuit constraints)
Step 6: settledEscrowSum = totalEscrow (passes line 443 check)
Step 7: _finalizeSettlement uses the accumulated sums. If per-batch distribution is wrong but totals are right, settlement proceeds correctly
Step 8: The concern is that a malicious oracle with a circuit bug could game per-batch values to produce incorrect totalLiability decomposition
preconditions: ZK circuit must have a bug allowing arbitrary per-batch value distribution while maintaining correct totals
Oracle must be malicious or compromised

title: RevealMarket._finalizeSettlement: totalLiability set from ZK proof output can exceed totalEscrow + protocolLiabilityCap, but the check is present; however individual batch signal[4] values are uncapped before accumulation
root_cause: In _verifyBatchProof (line 870), settledLiabilitySum += signals[4] accumulates liability from each batch. The ZK proof outputs are uint256 values that passed the SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD check in the verifier (Verifier.verifyProof line 108). However, the accumulation in settledLiabilitySum could overflow if signals[4] values are close to uint256 max. Since signals[4] < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD (~2^254), and there are at most MAX_LOCK_BATCH_COUNT=64 batches, the maximum settledLiabilitySum would be 64 * 2^254, which does overflow uint256. In Solidity 0.8.x, this would revert with arithmetic overflow. So an attacker cannot cause silent overflow, but they could cause a permanent DoS if the ZK circuit allows signals[4] to be very large. The _finalizeSettlement check (line 748) `required > totalEscrow_ + protocolLiabilityCap` would catch any excessive totalLiability after accumulation, but the overflow revert would prevent reaching this check. The real question is whether the ZK circuit constrains signals[4] to reasonable values. If signals[4] is constrained to be <= totalEscrow per batch, then 64 * totalEscrow << uint256 max and no overflow occurs.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market with 64 batches. Each batch's ZK proof has signals[4] close to SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD (~2^254)
Step 2: Oracle submits verifyAndSettleBatched with all 64 proofs
Step 3: _verifyBatchProof accumulates settledLiabilitySum. After ~4 batches, sum exceeds uint256 max. Arithmetic overflow revert
Step 4: Settlement permanently blocked. Market must wait for SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS then cancel via enableRefunds
Step 5: (Requires) ZK circuit to allow signals[4] values near SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD while still producing valid proofs
preconditions: ZK circuit allows arbitrarily large liability signals per batch
Oracle submits proofs with inflated per-batch liability values

title: MarketFactory.createMarket: No maxCommitments validation against zero allows market with maxCommitments=0 to default to MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT (16384), potentially exceeding pool capacity
root_cause: In createMarket, the CreateMarketParams struct has maxCommitments field which is passed to RevealMarket.initialize(). Inside initialize() at line 260-261, `if (params.maxCommitments > MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT) revert` and `maxCommitments = params.maxCommitments == 0 ? MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT : params.maxCommitments`. This means passing maxCommitments=0 defaults to 16384 (64*256). The factory at line 444-501 does not validate maxCommitments at all (no zero check, no bounds check). While the market's initialize handles the zero case, this means the owner can accidentally create markets with very large commitment limits. Combined with a fixed ticket size and liability cap, this is unlikely to cause fund loss since the protocolLiabilityCap bounds pool exposure independently.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Owner calls createMarket with maxCommitments=0, ticketSize=1e18, protocolLiabilityCap=100e18
Step 2: Market is created with effective maxCommitments=16384
Step 3: Total escrow could reach 16384 * 1e18 = 16384e18 tokens
Step 4: protocolLiabilityCap of 100e18 still bounds pool draws, but the market can hold far more collateral than the cap suggests
preconditions: Owner passes maxCommitments=0 (treated as MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT=16384)

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketRelayer: _activateRelayer called after registerMarket, but if registerMarket reverts, the entire transaction reverts -- no partial state corruption possible
root_cause: In updateMarketRelayer (line 279-298), the sequence is: (1) unregister old relayer (try/catch, line 288-291), (2) _deactivateRelayer old (line 292), (3) rm.setRelayerEscrow (line 293), (4) newRelayer.registerMarket (line 294), (5) _trackRelayer (line 295), (6) _activateRelayer (line 296). If step 4 (registerMarket) reverts, the entire transaction reverts, undoing steps 1-3. However, step 1 is in a try/catch, so if unregisterMarket fails, the old relayer is NOT unregistered. If the full transaction succeeds, the old relayer may still have allowedMarket[market] = true (if unregister failed). The market is now using the new relayer but the old relayer still considers it allowed. The old relayer's owner could potentially call commitOnBehalf targeting this market on the old relayer, but the market's onlyRelayer modifier (line 219-221) checks `msg.sender != relayerEscrow` where relayerEscrow is now the NEW relayer. So the old relayer cannot commit to the market anymore. The dangling allowedMarket entry on the old relayer is inert.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market M uses relayerA; owner calls updateMarketRelayer(M, relayerB)
Step 2: relayerA.unregisterMarket(M) fails (caught by try/catch)
Step 3: relayerA still has allowedMarket[M] = true
Step 4: relayerA.owner() tries commitOnBehalf to M via relayerA
Step 5: relayerA.commitOnBehalf calls M.commitWithAuthorization, but M's onlyRelayer checks msg.sender == M.relayerEscrow (which is now relayerB)
Step 6: Call reverts with NotRelayer -- no exploit possible
preconditions: Old relayer's unregisterMarket reverts

title: MarketFactory: Owner can grief users by pausing market commits and claims simultaneously, then sweeping unclaimed after claim deadline
root_cause: The owner can: (1) pause claims via setMarketClaimsPaused(market, true), (2) wait for the effective claim deadline to pass (claim pause duration is capped at MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION = 365 days, and claim deadline is extended by pause duration), (3) unpause claims, (4) call sweepUnclaimed. However, RevealMarket.setClaimsPaused (line 719-736) tracks claimPauseTotalDuration which is added to the claim deadline in _effectiveClaimDeadline (line 932-938). When claims are paused, the effective deadline extends by the pause duration. So the owner cannot shorten the claim window by pausing -- the effective deadline moves forward. When unpaused, the elapsed pause time is added to claimPauseTotalDuration (capped at MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION). This means the owner cannot steal funds by pause-unpause cycling because the claim window is extended by the total pause duration, giving users at least the original CLAIM_WINDOW_SECONDS minus any remaining time when paused.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market settles; claimDeadline = now + 180 days
Step 2: Owner pauses claims for 100 days
Step 3: Effective deadline = claimDeadline + 100 days (due to pause duration)
Step 4: Owner unpauses; users still have ~180 days from unpause (approximately) to claim
Step 5: Owner cannot sweep until effective deadline passes
preconditions: Market is in Settled phase

title: ProtocolPool.lpWithdraw: convertToAssets checked before idle liquidity, enabling state where assets > idle even at 1:1
root_cause: In lpWithdraw, assets are computed at line 253 via convertToAssets(sharesToRedeem), then idle is checked at line 258-260. When the pool is healthy (assets >= totalShares), convertToAssets caps at 1:1 so assets = sharesToRedeem. The idle check then becomes `sharesToRedeem > balance - reservedTotal`. This means an LP can be blocked from withdrawing shares they own if reservedTotal is high, even though the pool is solvent. This is the intended design (reserved funds are committed to markets). The lpWithdraw does not attempt to redeem against reserved funds. The only concern is whether the LP has any recourse if their funds are perpetually reserved — but releaseLiabilityReservation handles this when markets settle.
trigger_scenario: LP deposits 100, pool has 100 balance, 80 reserved, 20 idle.
LP calls lpWithdraw(50, 0). assets = 50 (1:1). idle = 20. 50 > 20. Reverts.
LP must wait for markets to settle and release reservations.
This is by design — LP liquidity is committed to market coverage.
preconditions: High reservation ratio

title: ProtocolPool._safeTransferExactOut: Recipient balance check can revert for hook-on-receive tokens when recipient is a contract
root_cause: _safeTransferExactOut (line 399-409) checks that the recipient received exactly `amount` tokens by comparing balanceOf before and after. If the recipient is a contract that triggers additional token transfers in its receive hook (e.g., auto-compounding vault), the recipient's balance could increase by more than `amount`. The check at line 408 is `recipientBalAfter - recipientBalBefore < amount` — it only reverts if received LESS than amount, not if received MORE. So this is actually safe for hooks that receive more. However, if the recipient's hook sends tokens back to the pool, the pool's balance check at line 405 (`senderBalBefore - senderBalAfter != amount`) could fail. In practice, LP withdrawal sends to msg.sender (an EOA typically), and owner withdraw sends to a specified address. The collateral token is set at construction and is expected to be a standard ERC-20.
trigger_scenario: Owner calls withdraw(to=hookContract, amount). hookContract has a receive hook.
safeTransfer sends `amount` to hookContract. hookContract's receive hook sends some tokens back to pool.
senderBalAfter > senderBalBefore - amount (because tokens were returned). Check: senderBalBefore - senderBalAfter != amount. Reverts.
Withdrawal fails. Owner must use a different recipient address.
preconditions: Recipient is a contract with token receive hooks that interact with the pool
Collateral token supports transfer hooks (e.g., ERC-777)

title: RevealMarket._verifyBatchProof: unchecked uint256 accumulator overflow in settledEscrowSum/settledLiabilitySum could bypass totalEscrow invariant
root_cause: In _verifyBatchProof (lines 869-872), the accumulators settledEscrowSum, settledLiabilitySum, settledPoolYesSum, and settledPoolNoSum are incremented with += from proof signals. Each signal is a uint256 constrained only to be less than SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD (~2^254). With up to 64 batches (MAX_LOCK_BATCH_COUNT), the sum of up to 64 values each up to ~2^254 could theoretically overflow uint256 (2^256). However, Solidity 0.8.x has checked arithmetic, so overflow would revert. The real concern is whether a malicious prover could craft per-batch signal values that individually pass the SNARK verifier but whose sum wraps. Since each signal must be < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD (~2^254) and max 64 batches, max sum is ~64 * 2^254 = 2^260, which exceeds 2^256 and WOULD revert due to Solidity checked arithmetic. This means a legitimate scenario with very large per-batch values would cause a DoS revert. But in practice, escrow/liability values are denominated in token amounts and would never approach these magnitudes. Additionally, the ZK circuit constrains these values to be consistent with actual commitment amounts, so the prover cannot forge arbitrary large values.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: A market is created with up to 64 batches (MAX_LOCK_BATCH_COUNT).
Step 2: The prover produces batch proofs where per-batch signals[3] (escrow) or signals[4] (liability) are very large values (near SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD).
Step 3: _verifyBatchProof accumulates these via settledEscrowSum += signals[3].
Step 4: If the sum exceeds 2^256, the transaction reverts due to Solidity 0.8 checked arithmetic, causing DoS.
Step 5: However, the ZK circuit constrains these values to realistic token amounts, making this scenario impossible for an honest prover.
preconditions: Market has many batches (approaching 64).
Prover would need to generate valid ZK proofs with inflated per-batch signal values, which the circuit should prevent.

title: RevealMarket._finalizeSettlement: pool.draw followed by surplus transfer and releaseLiabilityReservation -- draw failure leaves market stuck in Locked phase
root_cause: In _finalizeSettlement, if pool.draw reverts (e.g., due to pool being paused via drawsPaused, or insufficient balance), the entire settlement transaction reverts. The market stays in Phase.Locked. After the 14-day SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, enableRefunds can be called. However, ProtocolPool.draw (line 159) has a special bypass: 'if (reserved != 0 && (drawsPaused || marketDrawPaused[market])) -- the pause check is skipped when reservedLiability > 0'. Actually looking at line 159 more carefully: `if (reserved == 0 && (drawsPaused || marketDrawPaused[market])) revert DrawsPaused()`. So when reserved != 0, the pause is bypassed. This means once a market has reserved liability, the pool draw cannot be paused for that market. Good design. The remaining risk is InsufficientPool if the pool's actual balance has decreased below reservedTotal (e.g., due to owner withdrawals or other market draws). ProtocolPool.withdraw (line 194) prevents withdrawing below reservedTotal. But ProtocolPool.draw for OTHER markets (without reservation) could still reduce the balance. Actually, line 167: unreserved draws check `amount > balance - reservedTotal`, so they can only draw from unreserved funds. So reserved funds are protected. The only way draw could fail is a token transfer failure (very unlikely for a trusted ERC20). This is a well-designed defense.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market reserves 100 ZEN from pool.
Step 2: Pool balance is 500 ZEN, reservedTotal = 100 ZEN, idle = 400 ZEN.
Step 3: Other markets draw from idle, reducing pool balance to 150 ZEN.
Step 4: Settlement requires deficit = 80 ZEN from pool.
Step 5: pool.draw succeeds: reserved = 100 >= 80, reservedLiability decremented.
Step 6: If deficit were > reserved (100), draw reverts with ReservationExceeded.
preconditions: Pool balance is sufficient for reserved amount (invariant maintained by ProtocolPool).

title: RevealMarket._finalizeSettlement: poolYes + poolNo == totalLiability invariant is necessary but not sufficient -- does not verify these correspond to actual commitment data
root_cause: The invariant check at line 741 `if (poolYes_ + poolNo_ != totalLiability_) revert SettlementInvariantMismatch()` ensures the yes/no pool split sums to total liability. However, it does not independently verify that these values correspond to the actual committed outcomes in the Merkle tree. For example, if a buggy circuit output poolYes = 100 and poolNo = 0 with totalLiability = 100, but the actual commitments have poolYes = 50 and poolNo = 50, the invariant check would pass. The contract trusts the ZK circuit for correctness of the split. The poolYes/poolNo values are only used for the emitted Settled event (line 776) and stored in poolTotalYes/poolTotalNo. They do NOT affect claim payouts -- each user's payout is determined by their individual Merkle proof. So even if poolYes/poolNo were wrong, individual claims would still pay correct amounts (bounded by totalLiability via the claimedLiability check). The stored values are informational.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Circuit outputs totalLiability = 100, poolYes = 70, poolNo = 30.
Step 2: Invariant check passes: 70 + 30 == 100.
Step 3: Even if real values were poolYes = 60, poolNo = 40, claims are unaffected.
Step 4: Individual claim payouts come from Merkle proofs, not from poolYes/poolNo.
Step 5: totalLiability is the binding constraint for claims (line 470: claimedLiability > totalLiability).
preconditions: Circuit bug that miscalculates the yes/no split.

title: ProtocolPool.reserveLiability: market can call reserveLiability multiple times if the allowedMarket check is satisfied, potentially over-reserving pool capacity
root_cause: ProtocolPool.reserveLiability (line 116) checks `!allowedMarket[msg.sender] || msg.sender != market` for authorization. The market argument must equal msg.sender. There is no check preventing a market from calling reserveLiability multiple times. However, in RevealMarket, reserveLiability is only called from lockBatches (line 377), which can only be called once (phase check). So from RevealMarket's perspective, reservation happens exactly once. But if a different contract (registered as an allowed market) had a bug allowing multiple reserveLiability calls, it could over-reserve pool capacity. This is an IProtocolPool-level concern for arbitrary market implementations, not a RevealMarket-specific issue. For RevealMarket, the single-call guarantee from lockBatches is sufficient.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market M calls reserveLiability(M, 50). reservedLiability[M] = 50.
Step 2: Market M calls reserveLiability(M, 50) again. reservedLiability[M] = 100.
Step 3: Check: consumedLiability[M] + reservedLiability[M] + 50 <= liabilityCap[M]. Must still pass.
Step 4: reservedTotal increases by 50 again. Pool capital further locked.
Step 5: For RevealMarket, lockBatches can only be called once, so this cannot happen.
preconditions: A non-RevealMarket contract registered as an allowed market with a bug allowing multiple reserveLiability calls.
Liability cap must accommodate the total reservation.

title: RevealMarket.refundTicket: No accounting guard on cumulative refunds allows total refunds to exceed contract balance
root_cause: All three refund paths pay out the full ticketSize (line 520, 543, 558) but there is no cumulative accounting variable tracking total refunded amount (analogous to claimedLiability for claims). The contract relies solely on its token balance being sufficient. During the commit phase, rake is deducted: totalEscrow accumulates (ticketSize - rake) per ticket (line 318), but rakeCollected is also held in the contract. However, at settlement finalization (_finalizeSettlement line 761-763), the surplus (including rake) is forwarded to the protocolPool. If enableRefunds is called from the Locked phase (after lock, before settlement), the rake portion has already been deducted from totalEscrow but the rakeCollected tokens are still in the contract. So each refund of ticketSize should be covered by (ticketSize - rake) from totalEscrow + rake from rakeCollected. This works as long as no surplus was forwarded. But if enableRefunds transitions from Commit phase (where no surplus forwarding has occurred), the contract holds: totalEscrow + rakeCollected = sum(ticketSize - rake) + sum(rake) = sum(ticketSize) = N * ticketSize. So refunding ticketSize per ticket for all N tickets exactly drains the contract. This is actually correct. The real risk is: if enableRefunds is called from the Locked phase where reserveLiability has already been called but no settlement surplus forwarding has occurred, the contract balance should still be N * (ticketSize - rake) + N * rake = N * ticketSize. This appears safe because _finalizeSettlement (which forwards surplus) only runs on the Settled path, and enableRefunds blocks on Settled phase. So this is actually properly bounded.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: N users commit tickets, each at ticketSize = 1 ETH with 2% rake
Step 2: Contract holds N * 1 ETH (N * 0.98 in totalEscrow + N * 0.02 in rakeCollected)
Step 3: enableRefunds is called (from Commit or Locked phase timeout)
Step 4: All N users call refundTicket, each receiving ticketSize = 1 ETH
Step 5: Total outflow = N * 1 ETH exactly matches contract balance
preconditions: Market in Commit or Locked phase
enableRefunds called successfully

title: RevealMarket._verifyRefundLeaf: Merkle proof parameter is unused, enabling refund with arbitrary preimage on any commitment
root_cause: The _verifyRefundLeaf function (lines 926-930) deliberately ignores the merkleProof parameter (line 927: proof;) and only checks commitments[ticketId] == leaf. This is an intentional design choice: during refund, the caller must know the original commitment preimage (ticketId, outcomeId, amount, payout, salt, user) to reconstruct the leaf via _computeLeaf. The Merkle tree verification is skipped because in the Cancelled phase, the batched Merkle root may have been built incorrectly (as tested in testRefundIgnoresMerkleProofAfterLockedTimeoutCancel). However, this design means the refund path security relies entirely on the commitment preimage being secret. The refund function additionally checks _ticketOwner(ticketId) != user (line 515), so the caller must specify the correct user. The refund amount is always ticketSize regardless of what amount/payout values are in the leaf. This is actually secure because: (1) the user address is bound, (2) the full preimage must match the stored commitment, (3) the refund amount is fixed at ticketSize.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: User commits with known preimage (ticketId=0, outcomeId=1, amount=X, payout=Y, salt=S, user=U)
Step 2: Market is cancelled (enableRefunds called)
Step 3: Relayer calls refund(U, 0, 1, X, Y, S, emptyProof) - all preimage fields match commitment
Step 4: _computeLeaf reconstructs the same hash, matches commitments[0], refund succeeds
Step 5: User receives ticketSize (not payout) since refund is a full ticket refund
preconditions: Market is Cancelled
Caller knows commitment preimage

title: RevealMarket.sweepCancelledRefunds: Does not account for claimPauseTotalDuration in refund deadline check
root_cause: sweepCancelledRefunds (line 833-845) checks block.timestamp <= refundDeadline (line 835) without any pause duration compensation. Unlike the claim path which uses _effectiveClaimDeadline() to account for pause periods, the refund sweep checks the raw refundDeadline. The Cancelled phase sets claimsPaused = true (line 489) but there is no refundsPaused mechanism. This means refund deadlines are not extended by any pause. Since there is no pause mechanism for refunds (only for claims), this is correct by design - refunds in cancelled markets are always available within the refundDeadline window regardless of claim pause state. The claim pause only affects the Settled phase claim path, not the Cancelled phase refund path.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is cancelled, refundDeadline set to now + 180 days
Step 2: Claims are paused (but this only affects Settled markets, not Cancelled)
Step 3: After 180 days, sweepCancelledRefunds becomes callable
Step 4: No pause compensation needed because refunds are never paused
preconditions: Market is Cancelled

title: RevealMarket.enableRefunds: Cancelled market from Locked phase does not forward rakeCollected, leaving it available for refunds (correct) but rake is lost to protocol
root_cause: When enableRefunds transitions from Locked to Cancelled, it calls _releaseLiabilityReservation (line 496) to release the protocol pool's reservation, but does not forward rakeCollected to the protocol pool. The contract still holds the full N * ticketSize in tokens. The refund functions pay ticketSize per ticket, consuming the full balance. This means the protocol loses its rake revenue on cancelled markets - the rake goes back to users as part of their full refund. This is the intended design: cancellation is an escape hatch and users deserve a full refund including the rake portion. The protocol takes no cut on cancelled markets. This is economically fair but represents lost revenue for the protocol.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: 100 users commit at ticketSize = 1 ETH, rakeBps = 200 (2%)
Step 2: Protocol would have earned 2 ETH in rake if market settled
Step 3: Market is cancelled, all users refund ticketSize = 1 ETH each
Step 4: Protocol receives 0 rake from this market
preconditions: Market cancelled from Locked phase with committed tickets
